hero.heading: Why Ignoring a Ticking Noise Cost £2,500

content.text: Ford Ranger T6 3.2 Duratorq Oil Pump Failure Representative Case Study Why Ignoring a Ticking Noise Cost £2,500 A visual breakdown of a 2013 Ford Ranger 3.2 Duratorq oil pump failure: the ticking noise, the flickering oil pressure light, the seized engine, the repair options, and the decision that followed. "A ticking noise started on a Monday. By Friday morning on the M6, the oil light came on solid. Then a loud knock. Then silence." Compare Ranger Engine Quotes See the 5-Day Timeline 91,500 First symptom 92,000 Failure mileage £3,800 Final repair 5 days Noise to seizure 6 mo Warranty Case summary Five days from first tick to total engine destruction. The owner heard a faint ticking at idle around 91,500 miles. The oil level was full, so when the oil pressure light began flickering, they kept driving. The next day, the light came on solid at motorway speeds and the engine seized within minutes. Model Ford Ranger T6 Year 2013 Engine 3.2 Duratorq (Puma) First symptom 91,500 miles Failure 92,000 miles Service history Independent specialist every 12,000 miles Disclaimer: This is an illustrative representative scenario based on common Ford 3.2 Duratorq failure patterns, Engines Market 2025 quote-request data, workshop consensus, and known failure-pattern data. Individual outcomes vary. Early warning The ticking noise was not a tappet. It was low oil pressure. The danger signal was not low oil level. It was the pump losing the ability to maintain pressure, especially at low RPM and when hot. Monday Faint ticking at idle Audible when cold, quieter when warm, but never fully gone. Thursday Oil light flickered The dipstick showed full oil, so the vehicle was driven again. Friday Solid oil light, knock, silence The engine seized within minutes on the M6. If your 3.2 Duratorq ticks at idle or the oil pressure light flickers even once, stop driving and test oil pressure. A £50-£100 test can confirm pump failure before the bottom end seizes. Failure timeline 5,000 miles was not the story - five days was. From first tick to seizure took less than a week. The owner assumed diesel injector or tappet noise because the oil level looked normal. What the owner assumed "Probably a tappet or injector." Common diesel noise was assumed, not oil pressure failure. What was actually happening The oil pump was failing internally. Bearings starved, the crankshaft scored, and the bottom end seized. "The car still drove, but every journey sounded worse than the last." Symptom 1 Gradual loss of power over 3-4 days Symptom 2 Deep rhythmic knock, louder under load Recovery Flashing oil light on the M6, then seizure Workshop diagnosis The oil pump failed internally. The bottom end starved and seized. The vehicle was recovered to a Ford specialist. The engine would not turn manually. There was no blocked pickup; the pump had simply stopped maintaining oil pressure. Oil pump Failed internally - no oil pressure Crank bearings Seized and welded to the journals Conrod bearings Severe scoring with copper visible Crankshaft Scored beyond repair Turbocharger Unknown condition due to likely oil starvation damage Oil pickup Clean - no blockage found Specialist verdict "The oil pump failed internally. It stopped pumping oil. The bottom end starved, and the crankshaft seized. There's nothing rebuildable here." Replacement options Used, reconditioned, or new: three routes after seizure. Use the interactive toggle to compare the routes the owner faced after the seized engine diagnosis. Low-mileage used is selected by default because that was the route chosen. Supply cost £800 [INDUSTRY ESTIMATE] Warranty 1-3 months, supplier dependent Lead time 3-5 days Key risk Unknown service history and same underlying oil pump weakness Best for Budget-limited repairs or vehicles with low residual value Chosen route Low-mileage used engine £3,500-£4,500 Fitted cost with 3-6 month warranty. Better condition than a high-mileage unit, but no guarantee on the oil pump. Supply cost £2,500+ [INDUSTRY ESTIMATE] Final case cost £3,800 fitted Warranty 3-6 months, supplier dependent Lead time 5-7 days Best for Vehicles worth £8,000-£15,000 or owners keeping the truck 2+ years Most reliable route Reconditioned engine £4,500-£6,000+ New oil pump, bearings, rings and gaskets with a stronger warranty. Supply cost £3,500-£5,000+ [INDUSTRY ESTIMATE] Warranty 12-24 months Lead time 7-14 days Included Fully reconditioned long engine with new oil pump, bearings, rings and gaskets Best for Commercial users or owners keeping the truck 3+ years The uncertainty play The engine was replaced, but the turbo had also run without oil. When the oil pump fails, every component relying on oil pressure is at risk. The turbo could fail weeks or months after the replacement engine is fitted. Path A - chosen Fit only the used engine and risk the existing turbo. £3,800 If turbo fails later: add £800-£1,200 plus labour. Kept upfront cost down but left a known risk. Path B Replace the turbo preventatively at the same time as the engine. £4,500 £3,800 engine + ~£700 turbo. Eliminates the risk entirely. Fork in the road Scrap the Ranger, fit a cheap used engine, or spend more for reliability- The truck was worth around £8,000-£12,000 before failure. The owner needed it back as a daily driver and work vehicle, but did not have the budget for a reconditioned engine. Scrap the vehicle Path 1 Sell non-running as spares/repair. Return: £1,500-£3,000. Low-mileage used engine Path 2 - chosen £3,800 fitted. Chosen compromise for speed and cost. Timeline: 5-7 days. Budget could not stretch to reconditioned Why A £4,500-£6,000+ reconditioned route offered better reliability but was unaffordable. The owner agreed to change oil every 6,000 miles going forward. £8,000-£12,000 Vehicle value Truck value before failure set the ceiling for repair spend. 30-40% Repair ratio £3,800 was roughly 30-40% of pre-failure value - within the watch zone. Daily + work Usage The owner needed the truck back quickly as a daily driver and work vehicle. Limited Budget Could not afford £5,000+ for a reconditioned engine with new oil pump. Turbo unknown Contamination risk Turbo had likely run without oil; owner accepted future failure risk. £3,800 Total paid Low-mileage used engine fitted. Turbo not replaced preventatively. Low-mileage used engine - turbo risk accepted Final verdict The decision balanced vehicle value, budget limits, daily-use needs, and accepted turbo contamination risk over upfront savings. Outcome What happened after the repair- Six days off the road, £3,800 paid, and 18,000 more miles without turbo failure. Final cost £3,800 total Lead time 6 days Warranty 6 months Warranty result No claims made Long-term result 18,000 miles Turbo status No failure to date "Learn from me - if the 3.2 ticks or the oil light flickers, STOP. I should have stopped when the oil light flickered. A £500 oil pump would have saved the engine." Lessons learned An oil pressure light is not a suggestion. It is a stop-driving-now warning. If your 3.2 Duratorq Ranger makes a ticking noise at idle or the oil pressure light flickers even once, stop driving and test the oil pressure before the bottom end seizes. Oil pressure test £50-£100 Can confirm whether the pump is losing pressure before major damage occurs. Preventative oil pump £500-£1,000 Keeps the engine running safely if the issue is caught early. After seizure - used engine £3,500-£4,500 Car off the road for 5-7 days and short warranty. Reconditioned engine £4,500-£6,000+ Higher cost, but new oil pump and stronger warranty. A £600 oil pump replacement could have avoided the £3,800 used-engine replacement. An £80 oil pressure test at the first flicker could have flagged the failure even earlier.
